claims.claim: A correctly audience-restricted token for one resource should not work at unrelated resources.
claims.source_quote: A correctly restricted token for one resource should not automatically work at unrelated resources.
claims.claim_context:
ean?

- **An application's access token:** Its usable privileges depend on the intended resource and scope, and on recipients actually checking them. RFC 9700 recommends audience restriction, least privilege and recipient-side enforcement. A correctly restricted token for one resource should not automatically work at unrelated resources. A reusable bearer token is still a credential an attacker may replay where it is valid.
- **A refresh token:** This may allow replacement access tokens. Its client binding, granted permissions, rotation and expiry matter; it is not automatically an authorization grant for every service. These are protocol and configuration questions, not a property established by the word “OAuth.” [OAuth security BCP, sections 2.2–2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html#section-2.2)
- **An application session cookie:** A service can continue accepting that session after the initial login. That is also true for services you entered using a password and 2FA.
- **The Authentik SSO session:** This is the more relevant concentration concern. An identity-provider session can support new application logins without repeating authentication unless policy requires a fresh check. Application and identity-provider sessions have separate lifecycles. Compromise of the identity provider itself is broader still because applications trust its authentication assertions. These architectural consequences are distinct from theft of one narrowly scoped access token. [NIST SP 800-63B, sections 7 and 8](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#sec7)
